title: The Deception of Luxury
english: By misusing the immeasurable wealth of life, not using it, and acting lawlessly against Paul, they fight not with letters but with deeds. For he proclaimed with word what these hold and rule with works. When they appear clothed, they are seen like walls painted by passers-by. Even children stand around them, laughing at one another and pointing to the writing on the garments; and they walk past, not stopping for long.

There are lions and leopards, bears and bulls and dogs; woods and rocks, and men beast-slayers, and all the skill of painting imitating nature. For it was necessary not only their walls, as it seems, and their houses to be decorated, but already also their tunics and the clothes upon them.

As for those who are more pious than the wealthy ones, having reviewed the Gospel history, they handed it over to the weavers; I say the Christ our Lord meeting with the disciples, each miracle as the narrative has it: the wedding in Galilee and the water; the paralytic carrying the bed on his shoulders (Mark 2:1-12); the blind man being healed with mud (Matthew 8:1-4); the woman bleeding being taken by the edge of the garment (Luke 8:43); the sinful woman falling at the feet of Jesus (Luke 7:36-50); Lazarus returning to life from the tomb (John 11:1-44).

And doing these things, they think they are being pious and putting on garments graced by God. But if they accept counsel, let them, having sold those things, honor the living images of God. Do not paint Christ; for it is enough for Him the one part of the incarnation, humility, which He freely received through us, but carry the incorporeal Word mentally upon your soul. Do not have the paralytic on your garments, but seek the one lying sick. Do not constantly recount the woman bleeding, but have mercy on the grieving widow. Do not look carefully at the sinful woman prostrating herself before the Lord, but let the tear flow thick, being crushed by his own faults. Do not sketch Lazarus being raised from the dead, but prepare a good defense for your own resurrection. Do not carry the blind man on your clothing, but the living one deprived of sight.

Encourage with acts of goodness. Do not paint the remains of the dead in a flattering way, but nourish those who hunger. Do not carry the water-skins upon the garments, which He filled in Cana of Galilee (John 2:7), but give drink to the thirsty.

Regarding these things, the proud clothing of the rich man benefited us, and not only that, but also what follows. For luxury was added to the purple and the fine linen daily and brilliantly; yet, in both respects, it is of one single mind: to be adorned by useless vanity in delicacies, and to serve the palate and the throat with pleasant sensations.

Luxury, therefore, is a thing hostile to a virtuous life, signifying emptiness and dissipation, excessive enjoyment and a slave-like habit. And while the thing appears to be one, when examined in parts and accused, its composition consists of a diverse, greater, and manifold evil. For luxury could not exist unless increased by many materials. But as for accumulating the materials of wealth, one might without sin fail to lose nothing, unless, perhaps, according to the small measure, as with Job (Job 1:10), it should happen to one both to prosper abundantly and to live strictly according to justice.

Therefore, it is necessary for one living in luxury, first, to have a costly house, decorated with votes, stones, and gold according to the patterns, and to have it conveniently suited to the changes of the seasons of the year. For warmth is sought; the winter is wretched and turned away from the midday sun, having risen toward the North, while the summer is [warm], so that it may be breathed upon by thin and cold northern breezes. After this, there is the need for costly clothing for the beds, the couches, the mattresses, and the doors that are about to be clothed. For everything, even the inanimate things, is carefully clothed by those, as the wretched are stripped of their belongings.

Add to these also and consider the silver in the vessels, the gold, the expensive purchase of birds from Phasais, and the wine of the Phoenician, which the vines of Tyre pour out much and precious to the rich; and all the preparation of the rest of enjoyment, which those using it have carefully named. For luxury, increasing daily toward the more curious, already pours out the scents from India upon the faces, and more so, the perfumers serve the cooks rather than the physicians.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Poverty and Misery of Lazarus
english: Consider the crowd of attendants at a banquet: the table-preparers, the wine-pourers, the stewards, and those who lead them, the musicians, dancers, flute-players, comedians, flatterers, and parasites, following the trail of vanity. To acquire these, how many poor are wronged! How many orphans are crushed! How many widows weep! How many, being violently torn apart, rush toward strangulation. The soul of such a person, having tasted some water of Lethe, completely forgets who she is and with whom she is joined, and that she will one day be released from this union and, having been resurrected, will dwell again with the body. But when the time of the necessary and appointed command comes, which severs her from the fellowship with the body, a calculation of what has been lived enters, and a useless repentance occurs after the need has arisen. For regret is only a sorrow when the one reconsidering still has the power to correct; but when the activity of the one doing right has been taken away, sorrow is worthless and the change of mind is vain.

There was once a man named Lazarus (Luke 16:20). The word does not describe him as a mere poor man, but as one deprived of the necessities of spending and need, and also being tormented by painful sickness and having a body broken, homeless, unsupported, untreated, thrown at the gate of the rich. And with great care in the narration, he brings the misfortunes of the poor to a tragic climax, so as to expose the hardness of the one who does not show mercy. For he who suffers nothing from hunger or disease is an irrational beast, pitiless or sympathetic, a form badly shaped into a human, falsely pretending nature by his intention; rather, he is even more unsympathetic than the beasts themselves; for even pigs, when one is being slaughtered, are drawn to a certain sad sensation and trouble the butcher with their blood; but oxen stand by such a slaughter, empathizing with a sound, signaling the pain. And herds of sheep, when one of the flock falls into the clutches of wild beasts, fall into a state where the one held is being sought, and some mournful sound fills the air, seeking its kind and companion. But a human, the rational animal, who is day-by-day being educated in goodness according to the likeness of God, cares so little...

Oh, the relatives in the painful circumstances of misfortunes! Thus lay the much-painful and blessed poor man, not having feet, for he would have fled the insolent and proud one, having changed to another place; instead of the murderous gate, being deprived of hands by the closed hands of the poor, and not even having a palm to stretch out for a request, being obstructed by those very organs of the voice and producing a certain hoarse and rough sound of the sternum, simply maimed in all his limbs, leaving behind a wicked disease, a pitiful example of human weakness.

But nevertheless, not even such a list of misfortunes turned the Exalted toward a visit; rather, He leaves the man like a stone, unresolving the sin being perfected. For he did not have the common and respectable things to say to accuse: 'I did not know, I did not realize; the poor man eluded me, my mistress.' He lay before the gate, a spectacle of entering and exiting, so that he might work out the necessary judgment of the proud one. He desired even the crumbs of the table and did not even obtain these; but one was bursting from abundance, and the other was melting from want.

It was indeed good and just for that Canaanite, that Phoenician woman, to teach the wealthy misanthrope, saying those things written: 'O insolent and proud one, and the dogs eat from the crumbs falling from the table of their masters (Luke 16:21); but you did not deserve this gift for your brother, your kindred?'

But the dogs were carefully fed, especially the watchdogs; and they were worthy of a roof and a bed and had attendants appointed with haste, but the image of God was thrown down, neglected and trampled, which the Master Artist and Creator fashioned with His own hand, if Moses is reliable to demonstrate the origin of men.

If, then, the account of Lazarus ended thus, and such was the nature of things, as to describe our life by the irregularity of this life, I would have left great voices babbling, through which the created ones pass similarly, thus unequally among their kindred. title: The true meaning of poverty and the example of Lazarus
english: The poor man passes by sighing, having learned through his companions the blessed enjoyment of your fellow-sufferer. For you will find a precise judgment-court of the righteous Judge, in which the one who enjoyed pleasure sighs, and the one who lived in luxury is distressed; and each is carried to what is due to him.

And it happened that the poor man died and was carried by the angels into the bosom of Abraham (Luke 16:22). Do you see the ministers of the righteous and the poor, and the servants of the transfer? For angels were bearing him, looking at him calmly and gently, and by their appearance foretelling the healing and relief awaiting him. And he was placed, having been carried to the bosoms of the patriarch, which provides a starting point for the pleasureless to torture the depths of the Scriptures.

For if every dying person were carried to the same place, someone great would be a boundless bosom, capable of containing the multitude of the holy ones. But if this is utterly impossible, for a bosom, having been hollowed out, barely contains one man or with difficulty two, some divine vision receives us by the image of the sensible bosom, guiding us toward some intelligible reality.

What is being said? Abraham receives those who have lived a prosperous life. Tell me then, O law-giver Luke, as if to one present and visible, I will discourse with you: why, being among many righteous ones and elders of Abraham, did you allot this honor to the drunkard, remaining silent about Enoch, Noah, and if anyone else who was not following these during his life? But perhaps I understand you, and what I consider does not cast you out from your purpose.

Since Abraham is a servant of Christ, and this man received the manifestations of Christ differently from men, and the mystery of the Trinity was sufficiently expressed to us in the tent of this old man, when he welcomed the three angels as traveling companions; and simply, from many mystical enigmas, this man has become a familiar man of God, having later clothed himself in flesh and having clearly spoken to men through this human veil, therefore his bosom is like a pleasant harbor and an unshakeable rest.

He says it is the portion of the righteous. For in Christ is the salvation and the hope and the expectation of the coming age of all of us, through him having sprung from the flesh of Abraham according to the human lineage. And it seems to me that the honor concerning the old man has a reference to the Savior, who is also judge and rewarder of virtue, and with the therapeutic voice calling the righteous and saying: 'Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you' (Matt 25:34).

And the poor man came to die. There is a double significance concerning the poor man: one declaring the need of the necessary things, the other the moderation and the humility of character. Therefore, let him who lacks the things of the material world and labors for silver, being clothed in the garment of pity, claim the praise of virtue, and let him not consider the lack to be sufficient for salvation. For he who labors by necessity is not praised, but he who moderates his will freely is marveled at. Since for those who are destitute, if they have a way of life that is uneducated or uncontrolled, necessity becomes a supply for many and wicked daring acts. And I myself, all the wall-scrapers and men who walk on toes, and moreover looters and thieves and even murderers, if they ever passed by an official judgment, I have seen them as poor, unknown, destitute, and unhospitable.

From this it is evident that the Scripture now blesses that poor man who bears the hardships with a philosophical soul, enduring bravely toward the circumstances of life and doing no evil deed, so that he might be granted the enjoyment of luxury in the flesh. Whom the Lord also describes more clearly in the first of the beatitudes, saying: 'Blessed are the poor in spirit' (Matt 5:3). Therefore, not every poor man is righteous, but he who is like Lazarus; nor is every rich man rejected, but he who lives with such a choice of will as he who was contemporary with Lazarus; and of this, those who are witnesses through the trial of life are evident.
